initialMessages.content: Welcome to AlgoLens. I'm tracking your Quick Sort partition execution. Ask me anything about the current step, variable states, or why a specific swap occurs.
Why is the pivot always chosen from the last element?

Selecting the last element as the pivot is the Lomuto partition scheme. It simplifies the loop logic since the pivot stays at a known position (arr[high]) while the scan pointer j moves left-to-right. However, this can degrade to O(n²) on already-sorted input — that's why randomized pivot selection is preferred in production.

mockResponses: The current comparison checks whether arr[j] is less than or equal to the pivot. If true, we increment i and swap arr[i] with arr[j] to move the smaller element to the left partition.
At this point, i marks the boundary between elements smaller than the pivot and those larger. Everything at index <= i is in the correct partition side.
The final swap places the pivot at index i+1, which becomes its sorted position. This guarantees all left elements are ≤ pivot and all right elements are > pivot.
Notice how the scan pointer j only moves forward. This is what makes the Lomuto partition scheme O(n) for each partition call — it processes each element exactly once.
The swap you're seeing moves a small element from the right side of the boundary to the left side. Think of i as a 'write head' that tracks where the next small element should go.

Good question! The pivot value 10 is smaller than most elements in this array, so it ends up near the beginning. This creates an unbalanced partition — the left sub-array has only 2 elements while the right has 4.
Comparing with the Hoare partition scheme: Hoare uses two pointers moving toward each other, which typically results in fewer swaps. But Lomuto is easier to understand and implement correctly.
The variable i starts at low - 1 (which is -1 here) because no elements have been confirmed as smaller than the pivot yet. It only advances when we find a qualifying element.
